title: The oldest Marian prayer
hook: Sub tuum praesidium, found on an ancient papyrus: we fly to thy protection

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Memorare: a prayer that opens by reminding. Your line was never was it known. Did you notice a need before anyone named it? Day one thousand three hundred forty.

A scrap of papyrus, written in Greek, torn at the edges, with only parts of its lines left. On it, someone wrote down a few words of prayer, and when scholars pieced them together, they matched a prayer the Church still says. In Latin it begins Sub tuum praesidium. In the traditional English: we fly to thy protection, O holy Mother of God. No grand liturgy around it. No author's name. Just a handful of people, it seems, in some kind of trouble, running toward a mother. Today's word is the nickname this little prayer carries.
screen: `A SCRAP OF PAPYRUS, IN GREEK.` → `SUB TUUM PRAESIDIUM.` → `PEOPLE RUNNING TOWARD A MOTHER.`

segments.voice: First, the nickname, and its question mark. People call this the oldest Marian prayer. Scholars argue about how old the papyrus is, and the argument isn't settled, so it's fair to hold the nickname loosely. What nobody needs to argue about is what the prayer says. Second, the picture. We fly to thy protection. Fly here means flee: run for cover. It's the posture of the psalm about God's shelter, which in the Douay-Rheims says, "under his wings thou shalt trust." The prayer doesn't stand up straight and make a speech. It ducks under cover. Third, the name it calls her. Holy Mother of God. That's the title from the start of this stretch on Mary, the first of the four teachings. Here it isn't an argument in a council or a line in a creed. It's what people shout when they're running. The title is already a prayer. Fourth, the word we. The prayer never says I. Despise not our petitions in our necessities, the prayer goes on, but deliver us always from all dangers, O glorious and blessed Virgin. Not I. We. A group of people with real needs and real dangers, praying together. And the prayer is still being said: in Latin in the West, and in Greek and other languages in Eastern churches, at evening prayer and at the end of the rosary. Short enough to say in one breath. Old enough that its own age is a question. And plural, so that whoever says it today says it with everyone who ever ran for the same shelter.
screen: `A NICKNAME WITH A QUESTION MARK.` · `FLY MEANS RUN FOR COVER.` · `HOLY MOTHER OF GOD.` · `IT NEVER SAYS I. IT SAYS WE.` · then, large: `UNDER HIS WINGS THOU SHALT TRUST.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pray it once. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind a few people who are in danger or need right now: someone sick, someone in a war zone, someone who can't pay the rent. Gather them, in your mind, into one small group, the way the prayer says we. If you pray, say the Sub tuum praesidium once, slowly, in the old English if you know it: we fly to thy protection, O holy Mother of God, through to O glorious and blessed Virgin. Say it for all of you together. If you don't pray, hold that small group in mind for the rest of the sit, as if you were all under one roof in a storm. The bell holds the time.
The oldest Marian prayer. The nickname of the Sub tuum praesidium, found on a Greek papyrus: we fly to thy protection, O holy Mother of God. Today's word.
Your line: we fly to thee. Today, when you pray or wish someone well, say we instead of I, and mean the people beside you. Day one thousand three hundred forty.

howItsDone: Catholics pray the Sub tuum praesidium in Latin or English, sometimes at the end of the rosary or of Night Prayer, and Eastern Christians sing it in their own languages at evening services.

sources.ref: Sub tuum praesidium (Latin: Sub tuum praesidium confugimus, sancta Dei Genetrix; nostras deprecationes ne despicias in necessitatibus; sed a periculis cunctis libera nos semper, Virgo gloriosa et benedicta)

notes: The index title is a superlative ('The oldest Marian prayer'); the voice treats it as a nickname and says scholars argue about the papyrus's age. The usual identification is John Rylands Library Papyrus 470 (Manchester), with dates proposed from the 3rd to the 4th century or later; the script names neither the library nor a date. Confirm.
Hook: 'torn at the edges, with only parts of its lines left' describes the fragment's state; confirm. 'Scholars pieced them together' is general.

The traditional English ('We fly to thy protection, O holy Mother of God; despise not our petitions in our necessities, but deliver us always from all dangers, O glorious and blessed Virgin') is recited without quotation marks; its translation is not on the validator's list. Confirm.
Claim that the prayer is used in Latin in the West and in Greek and other languages in Eastern churches, at evening prayer and the end of the rosary: confirm phrasing.
Confirm Douay-Rheims (Challoner) wording of Psalm 90:4 ('He will overshadow thee with his shoulders: and under his wings thou shalt trust.').
Callback: 'the first of the four teachings' refers to day 1327 (Four Marian dogmas), Mother of God.
